title: Taps and capture
text: Your own code can tell you what it saw. Only the wire can tell you what actually happened, and when. This video is about getting that view, and reading it.

title: Measure outside
text: Timestamps taken inside a server leave out the time a packet spent in the card, the kernel and the queues. So trading firms also copy every packet off the wire, to a capture system with its own precise clock. The same clock then stamps what came in and what went out. Because one clock stamps both directions, its offset cancels out of the difference.

title: Mirror port or tap
text: There are two ways to get that copy. A switch mirror port, called SPAN, copies traffic inside the switch. Cisco notes that when the mirrored ports carry more than the mirror port can, drops occur at its egress buffer. A passive optical tap splits off part of the light instead, so the capture sees every packet, in order, without touching the link's timing. That is why trading firms prefer taps for latency measurement.

title: The pcap format
text: Captures are usually stored as pcap. A file starts with a 24 byte header. Its magic number says whether the timestamps are in microseconds or nanoseconds. Each packet then gets a 16 byte record header: seconds, the fraction of a second, the bytes captured, and the packet's original length. Storage fills fast at line rate, so a capture often keeps only the first bytes of each packet, up to the snapshot length in the file header. Tools like tcpdump and tshark read and write this format.

title: Wire to wire
text: Here is how a tick-to-order measurement works. Tap the market data link into your server, and the order link out of it. Match each order to the packet that triggered it, and subtract the two capture timestamps. Say the quote's last bit arrives at 0, and the order's first bit leaves 4.1 microseconds later. That is your wire-to-wire time, with the card, the kernel and your code all inside it. Do that for every order, and you get a distribution: watch the p99, not the average.

title: In the lab
text: The lab measures from inside. The feed's receive thread stamps every batch of packets with rdtsc, and that stamp travels with the data, even in the reserved field of each Aeron frame. LatencyHistogram prints the percentiles, from p50 out to p99.99, and the maximum. For the wire view, the setup script installs tcpdump and tshark. Comparing the two views shows where the time goes inside the box.

title: Takeaway
text: Software timestamps tell you what your code saw. A tap and a good clock tell you what really happened. Trust the tap when they disagree. Last in this series: how all of this fits together inside an exchange's data centre.
